extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school students and trainers preparing for mathematical olympiads (geometry, trigonometry, combinatorics)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, lemmas, and solution strategies for Olympiad-level geometry and trigonometry problems (concurrency, tetrahedra, telescoping sums/products, trigonometric substitutions, network-resistance combinatorics). Emphasizes method selection (vector methods, physical analogies, substitutions, telescoping, completing squares) to produce concise contest solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector face-normal method for dihedral cosine sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent dihedral cosines via dot products of outward normal vectors whose lengths equal face areas; derive identities such as S = 2 − (1/2)(v1+v2+v3+v4)^2 to bound the sum of cosines of dihedral angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vectors perpendicular to faces with lengths equal to face areas; express cosines as negatives of dot products v_i · v_j and manipulate sums to obtain inequalities. Equality conditions follow from vanishing of the squared sum (i.e., linear dependence/proportionality conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of face-normal vectors implies equal face areas
rubrics_metrics.description: If the vectors perpendicular to the faces (with lengths equal to the face areas) are proportional to certain constructed vectors, then the areas of faces are equal and equality cases can be characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After expressing aggregated vector sums, use non-coplanarity and proportionality arguments to deduce equality of face areas when the sum-based expression attains its extremal value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical equilibrium (gravitational potential) for geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Model points/masses at vertices and interpret the minimizing point of sum of distances/potentials as an equilibrium point; convert equilibrium of forces into geometric bisector/normal statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat potential as linear (first-order approximation) so the minimizing point is in equilibrium; equate resultant forces of vertex groups and deduce directions (e.g., bisectors) and concurrency by physical intuition backed by geometric construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsoid tangency argument for common bisectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ellipsoids of revolution by AX + BX = AP + PB (and similarly for other pairs); use non-overlapping interiors and tangency to show bisectors are normals to a common tangent plane and thus share a supporting line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct E1, E2 as in the text; use minimality of sums of distances to show interiors don't intersect, hence ellipsoids are tangent and their normals (bisectors) coincide at the tangent plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-of-mass / perpetuum-mobile contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use center-of-mass and physical impossibility arguments (a constructed body would roll forever if the point projected outside every face) to show geometric constraints on the location of a point relative to faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume contrary, construct an inhomogeneous polyhedron with the given point as center of mass; analyze its motion on a plane to derive contradiction, thereby proving the intended geometric property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optics/Fermat principle (river/bridge) reduction by translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Model shortest-path problems crossing a strip (river) as light path through a dense medium; use the fact that the path enters and exits at equal angles and reduce to a straight-line minimization by translating one city toward the other perpendicular to the shore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either use physical optics intuition or construct a translation of one endpoint by the bridge width (vector perpendicular to shore) and minimize the straight-line distance; deduce collinearity conditions for the crossing point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centroid division-ratio property for concurrency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the property that the centroid of k+j points divides the segment joining the centroids of the k and j point groups in ratio j:k to prove concurrency of constructed perpendiculars from centroids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute ratios G1G:GM = 2:(n−2) (or analogous ratios) and use similarity of triangles to show the constructed perpendiculars meet at a point determined by O and G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex-coordinate criterion for perpendicularity on circle
rubrics_metrics.description: For ω_i on the unit circle, the ray from the origin through ω_i + ω_j is perpendicular to the chord through ω_i and ω_j; sums like ∑ω_i/(n−2) lie on all such perpendiculars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complex numbers on the unit circle to translate geometric perpendicularity into algebraic relations; this gives an explicit common point for a family of perpendiculars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centroid-and-symmetry argument to prove regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centroid lies on perpendicular bisectors of segments determined by any two points, symmetry around those bisectors forces equal adjacent side lengths, hence S is a regular polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick three consecutive points and use symmetry of perpendicular bisectors to deduce equalities; iterate to conclude regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapse symmetric levels in hypercube resistor networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit symmetry: vertices at the same Hamming weight level have the same potential and can be collapsed, reducing the n-cube network to series/parallel combinations to compute resistance between opposite corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify levels (k ones, n−k zeros); collapse each level to a single node; compute series/parallel resistances yielding formulas that can be converted to combinatorial identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electrical-network / superposition methods to prove identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Model combinatorial sums via electrical potentials and currents; use symmetry and superposition to relate resistances across dimensions and derive recursive/combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set ground appropriately, compute potentials for unit currents entering/leaving specified vertices, then superpose solutions and compare with decoupled (or lower-dimensional) networks to obtain equalities like 2R_n − 2/n = R_{n−1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribing tetrahedron in a parallelepiped to simplify metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed a tetrahedron in a right parallelepiped (edges x,y,z) so that Pythagorean relations link tetrahedron edge lengths a,b,c with x,y,z and allow closed-form expressions for x,y,z and the tetrahedron volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write x^2+y^2=a^2, etc., solve for x,y,z (e.g., x=(a^2+c^2−b^2)/2) and compute volumes: volume(tetrahedron) = (1/3) volume(parallelepiped) = (1/6)xyz, leading to explicit formula via substitution and simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use circumsphere/parallelepiped diagonal relation for circumradius
rubrics_metrics.description: For a tetrahedron inscribed in a right parallelepiped, the tetrahedron's circumsphere is the parallelepiped's circumsphere; the circumradius is half the main diagonal, giving R = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pythagorean relations among parallelepiped edges; compute diagonal length squared x^2+y^2+z^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/4 and take half for the circumradius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection/orthogonality transfer lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Given point A and plane not containing A, with l a line in the plane and B the projection of A onto the plane, BC is orthogonal to l iff AC is orthogonal to l (because AB is orthogonal to the plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AB⊥plane to transfer orthogonality relationships from AC to BC and vice versa; apply to deduce altitudes and orthocenters in tetrahedral constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing tetrahedron orthocenter via altitudes intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct orthocenters of face triangles and show altitudes AH1, BH2, CH3, DH4 pairwise intersect and, since no three are coplanar, they meet at the tetrahedron's orthocenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use projection lemma repeatedly; show orthocenters of faces lead to concurrent altitude lines in 3D; symmetry arguments show a single intersection point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply parallelogram identity on faces to deduce edge equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use identity MP^2 + NQ^2 = MN^2 + NP^2 + PQ^2 + QM^2 on parallelogram faces of an inscribed parallelepiped to obtain equalities between sums of squared opposite edges and deduce orthogonality/length relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the identity for each face, exploit rhombus/right-parallelepiped structure to reduce to simple equalities like AB^2 + CD^2 = BC^2 + AD^2 and conclude desired properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhomboidal/right parallelepiped characterization to identify regular/isosceles tetrahedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate the tetrahedron's properties (equal face areas, equal altitudes) to the type of parallelepiped it sits in (rhomboidal, right, cube) to conclude when a tetrahedron is isosceles or regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine volume relations, equality of altitudes, and parallelepiped geometry; deduce that rhomboidal+right parallelepiped implies cube and hence regular tetrahedron in certain equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute tetrahedron volume via Heron + altitude from circumcenter
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute face area via Heron's formula; locate projection of an equidistant vertex at the circumcenter of the base face; compute altitude using Pythagorean theorem and combine to get volume formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute s = sqrt(p(p−a)(p−b)(p−c)), AO = abc/(4s), EA via rhombus geometry, then EO = sqrt(EA^2 − AO^2), and volume = (1/3) * base_area * altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping sums via trigonometric addition/subtraction identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use identities like cos kx cos x − cos(k+1)x = sin kx sin x (or sin(a−b)/(cos a cos b) = tan a − tan b) to turn series into telescoping differences and obtain closed forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply/divide by sin x or cos x as appropriate to produce consecutive-term cancellation; derive compact expressions like cot x − cos(n+1)x/(sin x cos^n x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arctangent telescoping with subtraction formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tan^{-1} subtraction formula tan^{-1} u − tan^{-1} v = tan^{-1}((u−v)/(1+uv)) to express sums of inverse tangents as telescoping differences, yielding simple closed forms like tan^{-1}(n/(n+1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express each summand in a telescoping form (e.g., tan^{-1}(1/(2k^2)) as tan^{-1}(2k+1) − tan^{-1}(2k−1)). Sum and cancel intermediate terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert trig sums/products using complex exponentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sin, cos via eiθ and e−iθ to convert products/sums into algebraic expressions or geometric series, enabling telescoping or closed-form evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write sines/cosines as (e^{iθ}−e^{-iθ})/(2i) etc.; use formulas for geometric sums and derivatives to handle polynomial-in-n factors; sometimes easier to see cancellations/pairings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-angle iteration to telescope infinite products
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the double-angle identity repeatedly to rewrite infinite products of cos(x/2^n) into ratios involving sin x/x or other limits; use limiting behavior for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply by suitable sine factors and iteratively apply sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x to collapse products; use lim_{n→∞} sin(x/2^n)/(x/2^n)=1 to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limiting sin x / x → 1 to evaluate sequences/products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a telescoping product/sum reduces to a factor like sin(x/2^n)/(x/2^n) as n→∞, use the standard limit to obtain exact values (e.g., sin x / x factors in infinite product evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the small-angle limit and apply it to remove vanishing factors in infinite-product computations (Archimedes-style approximations also fit this pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and term-pairing in trig sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit identities like cos(180°−x) = −cos x to pair and cancel terms in finite trigonometric sums, reducing the problem to a few boundary terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize sums so that terms pair under symmetric index transformations; often yields dramatic cancellations, leaving only a handful of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution to simplify inequalities and sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute x = cos t or x = tan t (or scaled versions like x = 2 cos t) to transform algebraic inequalities or recurrences into trigonometric ones where monotonicity, periodicity, or known identities apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose substitution suited to domain constraints (e.g., x ∈ [−1,1] → x=cos t with t∈[0,π]); convert recurrences into angle doubling sequences (tan 2α formula) to exploit periodicity and deduce exact forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity + pigeonhole on angles to force closeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Map numbers to angles (via cos/sin/tan), use monotonicity of trigonometric functions on specified intervals, and apply pigeonhole principle to guarantee angle differences below a threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the relevant angle interval into equal subintervals; two mapped angles must fall into same subinterval, giving a bound on their difference and hence on original expressions (e.g., sin(ti−tj) small).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Jensen/concavity on trig function sums
rubrics_metrics.description: When sums of concave trig functions appear (e.g., sin(x/2) on [0,π]), apply Jensen's inequality to bound averages and obtain global maxima/minima for constrained sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check concavity on the interval, replace average of function values by function of average to get upper/lower bounds; useful in bounding telescoped sums after trig substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence periodicity via tangent-doubling substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Set x_k = tan θ_k so that recurrence x_{k+1} = 2x_k/(1−x_k^2) becomes θ_{k+1} = 2θ_k; use θ_{m} = θ_1·2^{m−1} modulo π to analyze termination lengths or enumerate solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate algebraic recurrences into additive relations on angles; periodicity/termination conditions reduce to rational multiples of π constraints and counting modular congruence solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing squares to express polynomials as sums of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite polynomial expressions or systems as sums of squares (or sum of squared expressions) to deduce non-negativity and force each square to be zero to characterize solution sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try grouping terms and adding/subtracting constants to form perfect squares; when total equals zero, each square must vanish, yielding direct solutions. This is widely used in contest algebra to get uniqueness.
